prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength to reach unprecedented clock stability and accuracy

statement.case_for: I ranked circuit QED first in my opening ballot, but having read the full set of ballots I move B037 to the head of my preferred configuration, and I do so partly because of my own proximity to the circuit-QED community. The optical lattice clock is a clean, well-defined invention: the magic-wavelength idea removes the lattice light shift, which makes it possible to interrogate thousands of atoms at once, and the resulting 1e-18 level stability and accuracy has been reproduced and compared across several laboratories and species. It has opened new measurements, namely relativistic geodesy at the millimetre scale, tests of constant variation and searches for new physics, and a many-body regime of clock physics. It is the only candidate that two members placed first and four placed in their top three, and none of the seven members who ranked it raised a scientific objection. The two-person credit (Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking it to the accuracy and coherence frontier) is compact and matches the history as the colleagues describe it. I note that, as a theorist in quantum optics, I judge it by the clarity of the physics and the robustness of the confirmation, and on both counts it holds up.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are overlap and framing. Precision timekeeping has already been recognised through the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems, which included the ion-clock programme, and a committee may feel that the conceptual step from ion clocks to lattice clocks is evolutionary rather than a new regime. The credit for optical clocks is also not confined to two people, since Lemonde, the Paris group, other JILA and NIST contributors and ion-clock groups were all important. Finally, part of the prize case is about improvement in a figure of merit, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some of the impact is prospective. I rate these as real but not decisive.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B037 first as an unambiguous invention with extensive experimental demonstration, a clean two-person credit, and a timely position next to the redefinition of the second, while noting that the 2012 ion-clock prize overlaps.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific assessment and the two-name credit. I would sharpen one point on the overlap: the 2012 prize rewarded methods for measuring and manipulating individual quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock is a different regime, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated simultaneously with the lattice-induced shift cancelled. That is why its statistical stability is better, and it is not simply an incremental improvement on ion clocks. I would still like the committee to be able to state in the citation what is new relative to ion clocks, so I propose a citation built on the magic-wavelength lattice and not on clock accuracy alone.

responses.point: Lindroth put B037 first because of the close agreement between theory and experiment in precision atomic physics, and asked whether the credit should be broadened to include single-ion clocks given the 2012 prize.
responses.response: I would not broaden the credit to ion clocks. The 2012 prize already honoured the ion-trap work, and merging the two would blur a citation that is currently precise. I take your point that the concept of an optical clock is older than the lattice, but the lattice clock is what moved the performance frontier and is the more distinct achievement. Where I would qualify your view is on Lemonde and the Paris group: I think the committee should be open about the fact that the credit is not unique to two people, rather than claim it is clean.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first because it is a clear clue from nature that completes the electroweak sector, and the experiment itself has not been honoured after the 2013 theory prize, with the caveat that any three names are a compromise.
responses.response: I do not dispute the scientific importance, and I defer to you on particle physics. My difficulty is with the attribution. The discovery rests on thousands of people and on the accelerator, and the three founding spokespersons are credited for leadership of detectors rather than for a decisive discovery step. I think this is a serious and possibly unresolvable problem for a configuration of at most three names, and for that reason I would put B006 below the candidates where the credit can be tied to specific, identifiable inventions or observations. If you can show a defensible rationale for the three names, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked twisted bilayer graphene first for its quantitative theory prediction of flat bands, linked to a striking experiment, and ranked the topological-insulator entry second, while noting that the origin of superconductivity is unresolved and credit is incomplete.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the experiment is a very attractive story, and I have B018 in my top five. My concern is the one you raise yourself: the superconducting mechanism and the correlated phases are still debated, and the experiment was student-led by Cao, who is not in the credited names. I would prefer to wait until the interpretation is more settled, in the same way that the 2016 topological prize waited for a consolidated picture. I also share your reading that B042 and B012 describe the same field, and I would want one framing, so I would not combine them into a two-part prize.

responses.point: Mehlig placed active-matter hydrodynamics first as a simple universal mechanism, and placed the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological-insulator entry second as conceptually economical and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I am sympathetic to the topological-insulator case and ranked B042 third, and I accept your argument that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible trio. My reservation is the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission, which you also noted, because the HgTe experiment followed their proposal and the credit there is genuinely contested. On active matter I am not an expert, but I note you yourself say the precise exponents are only partly tested experimentally, and I would want to hear from you how robust the reproduction across laboratories is before giving it weight.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as a distinct new regime or as a refinement of the ion-clock work honoured in 2012.
Whether a two-name credit is enough given the contributions of the Paris and other groups.
Whether the timing of the redefinition of the second will strengthen or weaken the case.
Whether the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize makes a circuit QED prize premature, and how much weight my own field's proximity should have in that judgement.
Whether the Higgs entry can be given a defensible three-name credit.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue: I am director of WACQT at Chalmers, which builds superconducting quantum processors, and I am a close colleague of the circuit-QED and superconducting-qubit community. B008 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) is my own field, and I ranked it first in the opening round, so I flag that my views on it should be treated with caution and that I would recuse myself from the final decision on B008 if it were to advance. No specific personal or institutional connection to the credited names for B037 is apparent from my profile, but Chalmers has links to the Wilson/Delsing group and not to Katori or Ye.
